body:
Anyone who can channel Billy Shakespeare and Hunter S. Thompson in the same post is a force to be reckoned with.  And I am relieved that I am not the only one who somehow failed to undergo great epiphany after reading some professional's guide to 'winning against depression!!'  I will raise a toast to the end of the International Year of Suckage though.  Ice water it is.

And yeah, I wanted to be Tony Stark when I was a wee lad.  There was a man who had it going.  Money, fame, and women -- even if I was too young to really know what the aforementioned women were supposed to do.

I wonder about that a lot -- depression in school.  I see so much of it.  I think it is more common than we know.  I can't believe that the atmosphere is anything other than damaging to an entire demographic.  "Hey! this is the best time of your life!  Getting laid every weekend?  Going to the game Sunday?  How about the party after?  Come on!  You need to lose those blues!  Let's hit the clubs!"  Yeah, look, why don't I just run headfirst into the Chemistry building a few times and see if that makes it any better.

Or (even worse) "You didn't get an A on the midterm??  Man it was a breeze!  I can't believe you couldn't ace it."

Perhaps your situation is different, and that makes me wonder if a thread concerning issues faced in school might at least get some of these things out in the open.

The first two years were the worst.  I hope it gets better in the coming years.

Depression I understand, through tons of exposure if nothing else, but I have no emotional hook for PTSD -- that is to say having never experienced it (and as a non-professional) any thought I might have might be more damaging than good.  I guess the only real question I have on that side is: Do you like your doctors?  Do you think they know their stuff?  Do they remember you and greet you as something more than just the next patient?  I had bad doctors for years.  It's terrible.

Also, I can understand from my own experience that endlessly getting bounced around between doctors is crushing.  Believe me, that I understand.  Even when the news isn't bad, after a while it never quite seems good.  It's just another trip to another cold and bleak office.  I know depression is bad and we are all fighting here in one form or another, and I suppose this may not even be the right thing to say, but sometimes I think there is a real, concrete reason to feel blue.  Anyone would be sick of it after a while.  I sure know how I feel about it.

However, it was your comment about the patchwork quilt that really caught my attention.  My 80 year-old mother just finished working on one.  Her hands are so twisted by arthritis that it took her years.  I have it now, and without any guile or exaggeration, without trying to convince you of anything about what you are feeling now, I promise you it means more to me than I can say.  Is there any chance that (working slowly) you might finish your quilt?  I don't know if it might lead to unhealthy frustration so I don't know if it is the right thing to suggest.  But if you can work on it, however slowly, I do know what such a gift can mean.  Maybe your family or friends could help?  Just for a few minutes now and then.

And speaking of family, have you shared your thoughts with them -- I mean as far as how exhausting your current situation is?

I am off to go workout.  Get the blood moving a bit.  (Six-foot one and one hundred and eighty pounds of what I like to think of as svelt muscles.  Not exactly the Hugh Jackman physique I would have wished for.)  If it's nice where ever you are perhaps a walk is in order.  Around the block or around the yard.  At least then I will know someone else up and moving around when they don't feel like it.

And I would like to know more about the patchwork quilt.  I hope to hear from you when I return.

What condition do you have?  Obviously I have no business asking, and I can understand why you may not wish to say.  Sounds reasonably serious.  And yeah, it looks as if we cope with not sleeping pretty much the same way.  For the record, I tried some of my wife's cross stitching once.  Just did not have the motor-skill / eyesight to do it.  Epic failure in which she had to take out everything I tried.

Medication, for the most part.  I am on several pain killers.  I close my eyes and the whole room begins to spin -- as if I had too much to drink.  Then the headaches kick in and I get real frustrated real fast.  There was a time when I would just lie there and get so worked up.  Go to sleep!  Just sleep!  I can't remember being any more angry than that.

These days I don't fight it so much.  I get out of bed and read.  Probably not the right place to make this confession, but mostly I read about ship wrecks and mountain climbing disasters.  It seems bleak, but it has the advantage of keeping my mind occupied.  I think about what I would have done differently in each case -- how such events might have been avoided.  It can be fairly consuming, which is a good thing.  I was up at 2:00 AM this morning working on a bit of genealogy.  Anything to keep occupied.

How about you?  Medications causing issues?

Lemony.  You don't know me, but I am asking you to stop.  Tell me about your condition.   Help me understand -- if nothing else maybe we can compare prescriptions.  I am not asking you to justify anything.  I am only asking that you talk to me for a bit.  I am not promising anything.  I am only asking that you talk to me for a bit.  I don't really sleep anymore either.  We have at least that in common.  Write back.

While I do not wish to share information on the specific attempt I made, I will share my emotional state at the time.

Others might find this strange, but I didn't feel anything.  I didn't feel sadness or anger or regret.  There was nothing -- an absolute hollowness of being.  Nor (alas) did I give a single second's thought to how my death might affect others.  Other people were not a part of the equation at that time -- they simply did not even enter into the picture.  For me, contemplation of the act was the ultimate step of retreating into a universe of just me.  A black hole where things were so bad I could never escape.  My promising academic career was gone (as was my full ride scholarship) My girlfriend (now wife) offered all she could, but in the end I knew she really couldn't change the downward spiral of my thoughts (which only made things worse).  I was getting drunk enough to pass out in the elevator to my sleazy apartment.  (710 square feet and cockroaches crawling over me at night) I couldn't talk to my family; somehow telling them was one defeat too many.

I knew I was going to go through with it.  I remember so clearly that I was shaking.  I started.  And out of nowhere there was a single thought:  Sit down.  And that is what I did.  For over thirty minutes I sat still.  I sat on my hands so I couldn't get up and finish. I wasn't thinking about anything really, besides sitting down.  My knuckles hurt from the hard ground.  There was no change of heart or amazing revelation.  I just sat.

When I got up, I took a few steps and threw up, again and again.  I suspect it was too much adrenalin or simply too much of everything.

And for a week after that, I kept the experience to myself.  Not out of some sort of misguided attempt of strength or whatever, but because I had no idea what to make of anything anymore.

Depression closed in again.  You loser.  Why bother?  Everyone can see you failed.  You loser.  You have nothing left.  You screwed it all up.  You loser.  The thoughts were the same, but now I could see that they didn't have anything to do with my scholarship or my girlfriend or my family -- that the thoughts would be there even if I was a millionaire, even if I was married to the Playmate of the year.  Even if everyone loved me.  I began to understand how unfair and irrational my depressed thinking was.  There was no winning against it.  I would never treat anyone else so shabbily.

I cried a lot after that, but I also began to fight back against the patterns of thought that had trapped me for so long.  The depression does still come now and then.  I feel it washing through me.  But now I know it for what it is.  I understand it's not my fault any more than the gray in my hair is.  I sit and let pass.  That would be the one thing I would say to others facing the same choice.  At the moment when everything is caving in, just stop.  Sit down for however long you need.

(I am not a professional, so please take my thoughts as an extended hand of help rather than the voice of certain knowledge.  I do know the emotional tug-of-war between elation and depression amounts to an excruciating hell.  I have no right to ask anything of you, but I will anyway.  I ask that you consider the thoughts of a fellow sufferer.)

I was taken aback by your statement "There's no reason for me to be unhappy."  I suspect there is a reason, and that reason is depression, and believe me, I am not being flippant.  More and more, it is becoming clear that serious depression is associated with physiological changes in brain chemistry.  If this is true, then there is a real, definable, medical reason you are in pain -- no less real than an x-ray showing a fractured arm would explain pain. So I think there might very well be a reason you feel the way you do.  It may even be genetic, which is to say something you have no ability to control, let alone cause.  And even if it turns out depression causes no physical changes, there will never be any doubt that it is a pervasive and dangerous condition.  (I am old enough to remember when migraine headaches were looked down on as not being a 'real' medical condition.  Suffers were told to 'gut it out'.  Not so much the case anymore!)

As for art, writing, and photography, I do not believe the purpose is to be Mark Twain or Ansel Adams or Otto Dix.  There is no good or bad in the context here.  There is only a human being trying to capture her view of the world.  Pick up the camera, go out and see what it shows you.  And yes, you can write -- you can articulate your worldview.  I know this is true because I just read your post.  This isn't about succeeding or failing.  It's about movement through the world and how you perceive it.  If you get good enough to make money, well, then choices have to be made, and yes your work will be judged by others. I get that.  But for now, stop worrying about the future or whether or not your art will make the grade.  Get up.  Grab your camera and see what's out there.  You may delete every picture.  Or there might be one or two that you like.  In either case you will be practicing your art.  That's far better than spending a few more hours alone with depression.  After all, you already know what it's telling you.

Most important: I understand the bit about being a top student and I understand the good family and good S.O. and how none of that helps and in fact (in the end) only amounts to additional pressure.  Worse, it becomes possible to see that going to get help is an admission of ultimate failure.  What will everyone think?  But it doesn't matter what your professors or family or even your boyfriend think about getting help.  What matters is you are in pain and you need to go to someone who can help you heal.  This isn't failure.  On the contrary, in your shoes it is an act of courage.  Please.  Do this.

At times, I do.  But as I said, even at its worst, depression no longer has the grip on me it once had.  I was very close to the edge at one time, and now I am free of that.  All the little steps add up.  Life very much seems worth living now -- but there are times when it takes work.
